title: Classes in TypeScript
subtitle: Typed classes, access modifiers, constructors, abstract classes, and implements
author: KERNAL Team

whyItExists.problem: JavaScript classes have no access control — any code can read or set any property. There's no enforcement that a class implements a required interface shape.
whyItExists.solution: TypeScript adds access modifiers (public, private, protected, readonly), typed properties and constructor parameters, abstract classes, and the implements keyword to enforce interface contracts.
whyItExists.whenToUse: When modeling entities with behavior and state (domain objects, services, repositories). When you need access control or you want to enforce an interface contract.
whyItExists.whenNotToUse: Don't use classes just to group functions — a module with exported functions is simpler. Don't model simple data bags as classes — use interfaces + plain objects.

explainModes.beginner: TypeScript classes work like JavaScript classes but with labels. public means anyone can use it, private means only the class itself can use it, readonly means it can only be set once (in the constructor). abstract means 'this class can't be used directly — you must create a subclass that fills in the details'.
explainModes.simple: class C { public x: number; private y: string; protected z: boolean; readonly id: number; }. Parameter shorthand: constructor(public name: string) — auto-creates and assigns a public name property. abstract class A { abstract doWork(): void; } — can't instantiate A directly. class B extends A { doWork() { ... } }. class D implements Interface { ... }.
explainModes.standard: TypeScript classes emit real JavaScript classes. Access modifiers (public/private/protected) are compile-time only — the JavaScript output doesn't enforce them at runtime. For true runtime private fields, use # (native JavaScript private fields). Static class members: static count = 0. Getters and setters: get name(): string, set name(v: string). Class generic: class Box<T> { constructor(public value: T) {} }.
explainModes.technical: Implementing multiple interfaces: class C implements A, B. Class types: TypeScript generates both a value (the class constructor) and a type (the instance type). typeof MyClass is the constructor type; MyClass alone is the instance type. Override: override method() — requires noImplicitOverride tsconfig flag. Private fields with # use JavaScript's native WeakMap-based privacy — enforced at runtime.
explainModes.deepDive: Abstract classes can have both abstract members (no implementation, must be overridden) and concrete members (have implementation, can be inherited). An abstract class is unlike an interface in that it can have constructor logic, concrete methods, and state. Mixin pattern: function Timestamped<TBase extends Constructor>(Base: TBase) { return class extends Base { createdAt = new Date() } } — adding behavior to existing classes without deep inheritance hierarchies.

questions.question: What does `constructor(private name: string)` do in TypeScript?
options: Creates a local parameter named name, not a class property
Creates a private class property named name and assigns the constructor argument to it automatically
Throws a compile error — private is not allowed in constructors
questions.explanation: TypeScript's parameter property shorthand: using an access modifier (public/private/protected/readonly) in the constructor parameter list automatically creates a class property with that name and modifier, and assigns the constructor argument to it. It's equivalent to writing: private name: string; and this.name = name; inside the constructor body.

faq.q: Are TypeScript's private fields actually private at runtime?
faq.a: No — TypeScript's private modifier is only enforced at compile time. The compiled JavaScript has no access control. For true runtime privacy, use JavaScript's native # private fields: class C { #secret = 'hidden'; }. These use WeakMap-based storage and are truly inaccessible from outside the class. TypeScript supports # fields and enforces them at both compile and runtime.
